newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas free trade meeting not seen reaching deal.
newsitem.headline: Americas free trade meeting not seen reaching deal.

text.p: Ministers from 34 nations in the Americas meet here on Friday for preliminary talks on establishing free trade throughout the hemisphere, but they were not expected to reach agreement.
"It's impossible that an agreement will arise here," the secretary general of the Organisation of American States (OAS), Cesar Gaviria, told reporters on Thursday.

Ministers from all the region's countries except Cuba flew into Brazil's third largest city for the talks on Friday which will lay the groundwork for the next presidential summit of the Americas in Santiago, Chile, next March.

The trade and foreign ministers were expected to announce that formal negotiations for the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA), a project launched at the Miami summit in 1994, would begin after the leaders meet in Santiago.

But Gaviria said great differences remained between the United States and South America's Mercosour trade bloc, which groups Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, over how fast to proceed with the negotiations.
The United States wants everything from tariff reductions to subsidies to be discussed at the same time.
Mercosur, and in particular Brazil which faces a widening trade deficit, wants to split the talks into stages, with tariff cuts left until last.
At the official opening ceremony of the minister's meeting on Thursday night, Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso reaffirmed his country's cautious stance.
"We must not be in a hurry to advance. The FTAA which we want must not constitute a short-term victory for those who are looking for an immediate business deal," Cardoso said.
"The time we take to allow the FTAA to mature through careful and all-encompassing negotiation will not be wasted."
The FTAA dream launched in Miami envisaged the creation of a free trade zone of nearly one billion consumers and a gross domestic product in excess of $9 trillion by the year 2005.

Chief Argentine negotiator Jorge Campbell told reporters that deputy ministers meeting ahead of Friday's top-level talks had failed to decide whether FTAA signatory countries "will" or "should" start formal negotiations after Santiago.
There was also disagreement on whether the labour movement should be allowed a greater say.
Brazilian Foreign Ministry sources played down the possibility of a fiasco Friday.
"We have to wait and see what the ministers do," said one.
U.S. Trade Representive Charlene Barschefsky, Washington's chief negotiator, declined to comment.
Parallel to the official trade talks, more than 2,000 businessmen from across the Americas were debating the FTAA.
Brazilian business leaders said that there too, the U.S. and the Mercosur delegations failed to agree on how rapidly free trade should be implemented.
"Our rationale is not nationalistic. It is economic," Stefan Bogdan Salej, president of the Minas Gerais state industry federation, told Reuters.
"We have been through a chaotic market opening. If we have to open even more now, Brazilian industry won't have the capacity to stand up for itself," Salej said.
